questions.question: What is an MCP server, in plain terms?
questions.answer_summary: An MCP server is a process that exposes a set of callable tools/functions with typed inputs and outputs that an AI agent can discover and call during a task — often described as a 'USB port' for AI, standardizing how models connect to external tools and data.

questions.question: What problem does MCP actually solve for AI coding assistants?
questions.answer_summary: Out of the box, assistants work from stale training data and can't act on real systems; MCP servers connect them to current docs, actual files/databases, live browsers, and real dev tools so the model can execute, not just suggest.

questions.question: How is MCP different from plain function calling?
questions.answer_summary: Function calling lets a model express what it wants to do via structured tool requests within one provider's API; MCP standardizes how those requests get executed and discovered across many tools/services in a model-agnostic, portable way, reducing duplicated integration work as tool count grows.

questions.question: How is MCP different from closed plugin ecosystems like ChatGPT plugins?
questions.answer_summary: ChatGPT-style plugins are specialized tools in a closed toolbox controlled by one vendor, while MCP is an open standard any developer can implement and any compatible AI client can use.

questions.question: What real capabilities do MCP servers give a coding assistant?
questions.answer_summary: Examples include a Kubernetes MCP server for CRUD operations on pods/deployments/services, a GitHub MCP server for managing issues/PRs/branches/releases, and an AWS MCP server for managing S3, DynamoDB, EC2, IAM and other resources — all invokable directly by the agent.

questions.question: Can MCP servers help an AI assistant debug real running web apps?
questions.answer_summary: Yes — the Chrome DevTools MCP server lets an AI agent debug pages directly in Chrome, using DevTools' debugging and performance-insight capabilities to improve fix accuracy.

questions.question: Are MCP servers a security risk for AI coding assistants?
questions.answer_summary: Yes — compromised or malicious MCP servers can inject persistent instructions, exfiltrate data, or perform 'tool poisoning' by manipulating tool metadata/descriptions to trick the agent into invoking unauthorized tools.

questions.question: Has a real MCP server had documented vulnerabilities?
questions.answer_summary: Yes — in November 2025 Anthropic's own official Git MCP server was found to have path validation bypass, argument injection, and unsafe repo initialization flaws that, chained with a filesystem MCP server, could enable remote code execution via prompt injection.

questions.question: What is a documented real-world MCP prompt-injection incident?
questions.answer_summary: Docker's write-up describes a 'GitHub Prompt Injection Data Heist' where a malicious GitHub issue's text was used to manipulate an agent connected via MCP into leaking private repository data.

questions.question: Do I need to worry about which MCP servers I install?
questions.answer_summary: Yes — beyond malicious servers, every additional MCP server adds attack surface for LLM prompt injection, so server choice and permission scoping matter for security.

questions.question: How quickly can a developer build a basic MCP server?
questions.answer_summary: Tutorials demonstrate creating a first MCP server in about 5 minutes using scaffolding tools like create-mcp-server, since a server just needs to expose typed tool definitions with natural-language descriptions.

questions.question: Why do MCP tool definitions matter for how the model uses them?
questions.answer_summary: MCP tool definitions include natural-language descriptions the model can read and reason about, so the agent doesn't need the API hardcoded into its instructions — it can discover and decide how to use a new tool dynamically.
